faqs.q: What is digging the small sand mounds in my Inverness yard?
faqs.a: That depends on the shape. Eastern moles leave raised surface tunnels and small molehills, armadillos leave scattered digging in beds and lawn edges, and in sandy north and central Florida soils a southeastern pocket gopher leaves a row of sand mounds. A large burrow with a wide, half-moon apron of sand is different — that is likely a gopher tortoise burrow, which is protected, carries a 25-foot permit buffer, and must be left alone. Call us and describe the digging and we will identify it before any work is planned.

Inverness.wildlife_intro:
In Inverness, our crew's steady calls are raccoons in attics and chimneys, eastern gray squirrels at soffits and gable vents, and roof rats moving from palms and fruit trees onto rooflines. Opossums and striped skunks work yards after dark, armadillos dig lawns and beds, eastern moles tunnel the sandy ground, and Brazilian free-tailed and evening bats roost in older rooflines through the warm months. The county's habitat — spring-fed river towns, Gulf marsh coast, and low-density inland suburbs — and features such as Crystal River, King's Bay, Withlacoochee State Forest, Homosassa Springs keep that pressure close to housing in every season.

Florida has no winter shutdown for this work, so Inverness jobs run year-round, with the one hard legal gate being bats: exclusion is legal only from August 15 through April 15, and maternity-season bat calls become inspection and scheduling. Our crew works under FWC Rule 68A-9.010 with the property owner's authorization — Florida issues no nuisance-trapper license — checks any live trap at least every 24 hours, and seals the entry as part of the job so the next animal cannot use the same opening. Call us at (844) 544-3498 and tell us what you are hearing or seeing.

faqs.a: Crystal River pricing follows waterfront complexity: dock, deck, and boathouse gaps add to a standard roof seal, and springs-side corrosion means heavier materials. faqs.q: Is the snake by my Crystal River dock a cottonmouth?
faqs.a: Probably not — the dock snakes we identify here are usually Florida watersnakes, banded or brown, which are nonvenomous fish-eaters that flatten their heads when threatened and get misread as cottonmouths. A true cottonmouth is heavy-bodied, swims high with its head raised, and shows a dark eye band. Do not test it yourself: photograph from the dock at a distance and let us confirm. Venomous removals are specialist work, and harmless watersnakes are usually best left to eat and move on.

Crystal River.wildlife_intro:
Crystal River is manatee country — the springs at Three Sisters and Kings Bay draw winter herds and year-round attention — and the town's homes sit among spring runs, marsh, and the river itself. Wildlife calls here lean aquatic at the edges: raccoons raiding waterfront trash, roof rats in the older in-town attics, armadillos digging the sandy yards, and water snakes — harmless bands and browns, mostly — mistaken for cottonmouths along the canals. The Crystal River Preserve's marsh is never more than a few streets away.

Manatee etiquette shapes waterfront work: nothing we do interferes with the springs or the animals using them, and an alligator in Kings Bay is an FWC conversation, not a service. For homes, our focus is the roofline and the dock — sealing attic entries, screening the gaps under waterfront decks where opossums den, and checking traps daily. Springs-area humidity rusts cheap screening fast, so materials here are specified for wet ground and salt-tinged air.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Homosassa?
faqs.a: Homosassa quotes turn on the crawl space as often as the roof: skirting a raised cottage so opossums and skunks stay out is its own line of work, priced by linear footage and condition. We inspect above and below the house in one visit and give a single written figure for the combination your home actually needs.

faqs.q: Something lives under my raised Homosassa house — how do you get it out?
faqs.a: First we identify it from sign — tracks in the sand, scat, and the size of the dug entry — because opossum, skunk, and armadillo each call for a different approach. Then we fit a one-way door or trap at the active opening, confirm the space is empty, and skirt the foundation with buried-edge screening so the next animal cannot dig back in. Simply boarding the hole without confirming it is empty traps animals underneath, which is the one outcome worse than the original problem.

Homosassa.wildlife_intro:
Homosassa — Old Homosassa's fishing village streets and the newer Homosassa Springs subdivisions — sits where the river meets the Gulf marsh, and its wildlife is marsh-flavored. Raccoons work the crab traps and trash along Fishbowl Drive, opossums den under the village's raised cottages, roof rats occupy the palms, and armadillos churn the shell-road yards. The state park's springs and the Chassahowitzka refuge to the south keep wild cover close on every side.

Village homes on piers and blocks are a specialty: the crawl space under a raised Homosassa house is prime opossum and skunk habitat, and screening that skirt properly ends most of the nighttime thumping. Skunk work starts with identification — striped skunks are the routine removal; a spotted skunk, a Florida conservation-concern species, gets confirmed and handled gently. Riverfront callers also ask about otters under docks: those are wild neighbors to enjoy, not nuisance bookings, unless one takes up residence in a boathouse, which we assess honestly.

faqs.q: What is making the sand mounds in my Lecanto yard?
faqs.a: On Lecanto's sandy ground the usual author is the southeastern pocket gopher — a burrowing rodent that pushes up fan-shaped mounds of loose sand, each with a plugged hole off to one side. It is not a mole (moles leave raised surface tunnels and small volcano-shaped hills) and it is not a gopher tortoise, whose burrow is a single large half-moon opening with a broad apron, protected by law. Pocket gophers are lawful yard work; we will confirm the mound pattern on inspection and lay out the trapping plan.

Lecanto.wildlife_intro:
Lecanto is Citrus County's inland center — government complex, hospital, college campus, and subdivisions spread through rolling oak and pine country along the SR-44 corridor. Away from the coast, the calls shift: gray squirrels in the oak-shaded attics, armadillos and eastern moles tearing up the big lots, raccoons in the dumpsters and chimneys, and southeastern pocket gopher mounds puzzling new homeowners who moved from the coast. The Withlacoochee State Forest is the county's eastern wall.

Inland Citrus work leans on yard diagnosis. Three different animals make three different mounds and tunnels here — mole ridges, pocket gopher sand fans, armadillo digs — plus the protected fourth, the gopher tortoise burrow, which we identify and refer rather than touch. Getting that ID right in Lecanto saves homeowners from paying for the wrong treatment, and it is where our inspection earns its fee before any trap is discussed.

faqs.q: What should I do about armadillo digging in Beverly Hills?
faqs.a: Nine-banded armadillos dig for grubs and earthworms in lawns and flower beds, and they are common throughout most of Florida, including Beverly Hills. A live-trapped armadillo may be released on-site, or released within the same county on 40 or more contiguous acres with the landowner's written permission, within 24 hours — those are the Florida rules, and we follow them. We also talk through fencing and grub management, because trapping alone rarely ends digging in good habitat.

faqs.q: Armadillos keep digging up our Beverly Hills lawn and under the porch. How do you stop the cycle?
faqs.a: By closing the burrows, not just catching the digger. Armadillos here work a home range and return to proven burrows; an emptied burrow under your porch is an advertisement to the next one. We trap the animals working your property, then backfill and screen the burrow openings and check the slab and driveway edges for the undermining that matters. On the lawn side, we will tell you honestly if a heavy grub load is feeding the digging — treating the food source and trapping together ends the cycle faster than either alone.

faqs.q: Our Beverly Hills home is empty all summer. What should be done before we leave?
faqs.a: A pre-departure seal, ideally in the spring before you go. We inspect the whole roofline — soffit vents, gable vents, the carport and Florida room junctions that are the standard entries on homes of this era — exclude anything already in residence, and close every opening in metal and screen. Raccoons and free-tailed bats claim quiet houses over the summer precisely because nothing disturbs them; a sealed house is simply not available to claim. We document the work with photos so you can see the closed entries from up north.

Beverly Hills is not a town and has no downtown — it is one of Florida's great postwar subdivision landscapes, thousands of modest ranch homes laid out in the 1960s and 70s across the sandy Citrus County hills, and its wildlife work is the work of an ageing suburb surrounded by forest. The Withlacoochee State Forest stands at its edges, and from that forest come the raccoons in the chimneys and attics, the gray squirrels in the oak hammocks' canopy streets, and the armadillos that treat every irrigated lawn in the community as a grub farm. Eastern moles run the sandy soil so thoroughly here that a street can share one continuous tunnel system argument for weeks.

The homes themselves are the other half of the pattern. Original-era ranch houses are now fifty-plus years old: soffits and fascia at the end of their second life, carports and Florida rooms added across the decades, and crawlspaces and slab edges the armadillos test nightly. Beverly Hills also has an older population that spends winters elsewhere — snowbird homes sit closed for months, and a closed ranch house in armadillo-and-raccoon country is a den with utilities. Our inspections here are built for that reality: whole-roofline reads, not single holes.
Beverly Hills.extendedBody:
The ranch-house roofline, fifty years on

A 1968 ranch home presents a specific set of wildlife doors: the soffit vents that were screened with material long since rusted through, the gable vents, the junction where the carport or Florida room roof meets the original house, and the plumbing and AC penetrations nobody has looked at since the Clinton administration. Gray squirrels work the canopy streets and chew in at those junctions; raccoons take the chimneys and the bigger failures. Our Beverly Hills inspections are systematic for a reason — on a street of identical-era homes, the animal is rarely using an exotic entry; it is using the standard one, and the standard one exists on every house of the same vintage until somebody closes it properly.

Armadillos and moles: the sandy-soil constant

Beverly Hills' other signature is underground. Armadillos root the lawns for grubs and dig their burrows under porches, driveways, and AC pads — an open burrow here gets claimed by the next armadillo, or by a skunk or opossum, so we trap the resident and backfill and screen the openings in the same job. Moles tunnel the sand in long feeding systems that surface as the ridged runs crossing whole yards. Our work is done under FWC Rule 68A-9.010 with the property owner's authorization — Florida issues no nuisance-trapper license — and where a native animal is relocated, it is only on the rule's strict terms: same county, forty-plus contiguous acres, the receiving landowner's written permission, within a day.

Snowbird homes and the closed-house problem

A Beverly Hills home closed from May to October gives a raccoon or a bat colony an undisturbed season, and the discovery in November is never just an animal — it is a season of droppings in the attic and damage at the entries. We seal these homes to be empty: caps, screens, and metal at every standard entry, so the house that gets opened in the fall is the house that was closed in the spring. For owners up north, we document what was found and what was closed, with photos, because a report you can read beats a bill you cannot verify.
